assessmentSummary.identity: A planned short approach into an approximately 45-degree sidestep redirection followed by a deliberately held terminal position. The proposed baseline uses the foot opposite the new direction as the main cut plant, redirects toward a marked exit lane, and stops on the first exit step for a two-second hold. The exact historical meaning of stick—holding the cut plant versus holding the first exit contact—remains a required human identity decision.
currentCardFindings: 45-Degree Cut to Stick is a direct wording duplicate and is consolidated into this identity; its rotational-source profile remains traceable as a source-context variant.
The existing card names a 45-degree route but does not define approach distance, approach speed, cut technique, plant side, terminal foot, hold duration, or valid lane tolerance.

The current physical score does not distinguish low-speed teaching from fast body-mass braking; the proposed baseline score assumes a controlled three-to-five-meter approach rather than maximal entry speed.
No existing video is approved. The four candidates include 45-degree cutting and deceleration components, but none is asserted to show the exact proposed held terminal contact.

coachCues: Push the ground away from the new direction
athleteInstructions: Approach the cut marker at the assigned speed
Use the last steps to lower and control speed
Plant the foot opposite the new direction
Stop on the assigned terminal foot and hold for two seconds

calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: Published studies define a 45-degree sidestep cut but do not define this library card's word stick. The proposed first-exit-contact hold is an explicit candidate interpretation, not an externally verified historical definition.

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain one consolidated 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick definition. Before publication, a domain coach must declare whether the hold occurs on the cut plant or first exit contact; the instructions, media, measurement, and profile must all bind to that exact version.

currentCardSnapshot.description: 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick is a cone-based athletic drill focused on controlled angled cut entry and exit posture. Start cone, approach cone, and exit cone set at a 45-degree angle. It belongs in the library because it is easy to set up, easy to coach, and scalable from youth development to advanced field/court athletes.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Youth training requires qualified supervision, technically appropriate progression, safe environments, and attention to individual readiness.
Stop 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick for pain, guarding, slipping, repeated loss of alignment or balance, unsafe lane traffic, or a material decline in the assigned movement quality.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Youth development should be individualized, progressive, and based on current physical and psychosocial readiness rather than a fixed exercise-card level.

Make 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick accessible with a walk-through, shorter approach or projection, lower speed, visible floor arrows, longer reset, and a simpler prerequisite task; do not label the exercise itself beginner or advanced.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.
The supplied links are candidate demonstrations only. oEmbed availability was checked, but exact sequence, safety, cue quality, captions, full content, reviewer identity, and approval remain pending.
The NSCA run-and-cut drill uses an approach, a cut step, and an approximately 45-degree exit, establishing approach, plant, and exit direction as the base sequence.
Adding a deliberate held terminal contact distinguishes 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick from the NSCA drill's immediate acceleration; the exact held contact must be declared before publication.

evidence.sourceTitle: Center of mass direction and speed during a 45-degree change of direction task performed with maximal effort
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: A maximal 45-degree change of direction distributes directional change across approach, execution, and following steps rather than one isolated plant.
Taxonomy for 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick must record approach, cut technique, angle, plant side, terminal contact, and held outcome instead of treating the drill as a generic cone cut.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of foot strike patterns and angles on the biomechanics of side-step cutting
claims: Forty-five-degree sidestep cutting involves ankle, knee, and hip kinematics, kinetics, and lower-limb muscle activity during the loading phase.

The card should represent ankle and subtalar stabilization, knee and hip force acceptance, pelvis and trunk control, and plantarflexor, hamstring, quadriceps, gluteal, and frontal-plane stabilizer contributions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Center of mass direction and speed during a 45-degree change of direction task performed with maximal effort
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: At high approach speed, only part of the required 45-degree redirection occurs during the main execution step; adjacent steps share redirection and acceleration demands.
Coach braking across the approach rather than demanding one hard last-step stop, and measure the actual exit path rather than assuming the plant alone creates 45 degrees.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Determinants of Performance and Injury Risk During Cutting: A Performance-Injury Conflict?
claims: Cutting performance and injury-related mechanics reflect interacting whole-body and joint strategies and vary with task demands.

Assess technical complexity and body-mass braking demand directly for 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick; keep coordination, supervision, consequence, impact, and work capacity separate, and derive overall from technical and physical difficulty.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports
claims: Horizontal deceleration requires high eccentric braking forces distributed across multiple steps and is affected by approach momentum and task constraints.

Track approach speed, cut contacts, direction, surface, extra stabilization contacts, asymmetry, and other session sprint or change-of-direction exposure; do not infer low physical demand from the absence of external load.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of the Cutting Alignment Scoring Tool (CAST) to Assess Trunk and Limb Alignment During a 45-Degree Side-Step Cut
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: A 45-degree sidestep-cut assessment depends on a standardized approach and visible trunk and lower-limb alignment.
45-Degree Cut-and-Stick needs a marked approach, cut point, 45-degree exit lane, adequate runoff, a high-traction surface, and observation angles that reveal trunk, hip, knee, and foot alignment.
The professional drill alternates right and left cuts and emphasizes immediate technical execution rather than fatigue accumulation.
The proposed low-repetition bilateral dose and full reset are conservative coaching inferences; no cited source validates one universal dose for this exact held variant.
The NSCA description specifies approach deceleration, a cut step, body weight inside the base of support, and an approximately 45-degree exit.
Instructions must additionally name the cut foot, exit lane, declared terminal contact, hold duration, valid repetition, reset, and direction alternation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Determinants of Performance and Injury Risk During Cutting: A Performance-Injury Conflict?
claims: Planned side-step mechanics should be developed before adding unanticipated stimuli and sport-like perceptual complexity.
Use 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick as planned braking and control practice, not as a reactive-agility test, maximal speed test, or conditioning circuit.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of the Cutting Alignment Scoring Tool (CAST) to Assess Trunk and Limb Alignment During a 45-Degree Side-Step Cut
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Qualitative 45-degree cutting assessment observes trunk lean, cut width, knee position, and related alignment features.
Athlete support needs a top-down route diagram, side-specific plant cue, terminal-foot target, two-second count, successful versus failed examples, and pain or confidence stop guidance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of the Cutting Alignment Scoring Tool (CAST) to Assess Trunk and Limb Alignment During a 45-Degree Side-Step Cut
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: The Cutting Alignment Scoring Tool provides a structured qualitative approach to observing trunk and lower-limb alignment during a 45-degree sidestep cut.
Coach support should standardize entry speed and lane geometry, compare both sides, observe from front-oblique and rear views, log extra contacts, and regress speed before changing angle.

evidence.sourceTitle: Center of mass direction and speed during a 45-degree change of direction task performed with maximal effort
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: The physical solution to a 45-degree task includes approach, execution, and following-step contributions.
Changing terminal outcome, cut angle, cue predictability, cut technique, or entry locomotion must be classified explicitly; punctuation or and-versus-to wording is the same identity.

alternateAssessments.name: 45-Degree Cut to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: And versus to wording does not change the planned approach, 45-degree redirection, or deliberate held terminal outcome.

alternateAssessments.name: 45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate
alternateAssessments.rationale: Immediate acceleration changes the terminal outcome, force sequence, measurement, dose, and phase intent from control to output.

alternateAssessments.name: Reactive-Cue 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: An unpredictable left-right cue adds perception and decision demand while preserving the same physical route and held finish.

alternateAssessments.name: Crossover 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: Changing from sidestep plant to crossover technique changes footwork and joint-loading strategy but can remain a reviewed technique variant under the same route and outcome.

alternateAssessments.name: 90-Degree Cut-and-Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: A 90-degree task changes braking demand, directional impulse, joint mechanics, lane layout, and transfer.
